newsitem.title: ALBANIA: OSCE's Vranitzky works on Albanian vote problems.
newsitem.headline: OSCE's Vranitzky works on Albanian vote problems.

text.p: Former Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky met senior Albanian politicians on Wednesday, four days before a general election, to iron out procedural problems threatening to spoil the vote after months of violence.

Vranitzky heads a mission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) overseeing Sunday's election, widely viewed as a public judgment of President Sali Berisha's five years in office.

Vranitzky met two top officials of the Socialist Party challenging Berisha's Democratic Party in the vote -- Prime Minister Bashkim Fino and Socialist leader Fatos Nano. Talks focused on two unsolved problems -- polling hours and how to distribute 40 seats to be decided by proportional voting.
"A lot of different viewpoints were expressed in the talks and things weren't always easy," a diplomatic source said.
"Vranitzky also talked about what would happen after the election. He wants some assurance that both sides will accept the outcome of the vote and not unleash new violence."
Some 1,500 people have died since unrest began in January after hundreds of thousands of investors lost life savings in the collapse of fraudulent "pyramid" investment schemes.
The diplomatic source said Vranitzky was determined to resolve the two issues when he meets Berisha on Thursday.

Major parties have agreed to close polling stations at 6 p.m., three hours early, to reduce the possibility of cheating and help 450 election monitors oversee procedures. But Berisha says he has no authority to issue the necessary decree.
No consensus has been reached on the 40 proportional seats after a court threw out a proposal to guarantee smaller parties a fixed number. Two-round majority races will decide 115 seats.
Berisha called the early election at the height of the disturbances in March and also had to appoint an all-party government headed by his Socialist rivals.
The president is not up for re-election but has been campaigning hard to defend the big majority won by his party in last year's election now widely denounced as unfair.
A 7,000-strong international peacekeeping force has maintained a degree of order since March but some regions are still outside authorities' control. Several dozen people have died in the past week.
As Vranitzky arrived, fresh political infighting erupted between Berisha's Democrats and the Socialists.
Prime Minister Fino, a Socialist, refused to sign a presidential decree on controlling investment funds. Five five shady pyramid schemes collapsed earlier this year, triggering the violence.
Berisha signed the decree this week in response to an appeal from the heads of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank to act quickly to quell unrest.

Finance Minister Arben Malaj, also a Socialist, said the president had altered key points of a proposed text put forth by the government. He said there was now little hope of resolving the standoff before the election.
In the absence of proper opinion polls, it is virtually impossible to predict the outcome of Sunday's vote. Both Berisha's Democrats and the Socialists have predicted victory.
Albanians will also vote in a referendum on whether to restore the monarchy.

About 3,000 people gathered at a monarchist rally in Tirana's central Skanderbeg Square, but King Leka, back in Albania after 58 years in exile, made only a brief address to seek support to return him to the throne.
